solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; the grid proves the blog's enumeration wrong at 9 across, recounted from the answer here

clue.text: Revolutionary essence derived from turning over leaf

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns right round, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: an essence extracted from a plant is named 'oil of' it, as in oil of cloves

explanation.surface: A radical extract obtained by turning over a leaf, like some herbal remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'oil of' stands for an essence derived from something; written backwards it becomes FOLIO.
explanation.definitionFit: A folio is a single sheet of a book or manuscript, numbered on one side only, which is what a leaf means.

clue.text: Man with secret order to release mother and child

blocks.note: to release is to set free
an informal word for mother
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A man in a clandestine organisation is ordered to set a mother and her child free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secret order' is read as a command in the surface, but in the definition it is a society whose rituals are kept private.
explanation.definitionFit: Freemasons belong to a fraternal society famous for its private rituals, so a member is a man with a secret order.

clue.text: Top copper’s held up, that’s clear

indicators.note: whatever is held sits inside the thing holding it
in a vertical entry, going upward means the letters are written in the opposite order

blocks.note: a lid is the top of a container
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A senior policeman has been delayed, and that much is obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top copper' looks like one phrase for a chief constable, but it splits: Top is LID and copper is the metal, whose symbol CU goes in upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucid writing or speech is easy to understand, which is one of the senses of clear.

clue.text: Make too much of frequency of deliveries

blocks.note: first meaning: to value something more highly than it deserves
second meaning, read as two words: the cricket term for how quickly a team bowls its overs

explanation.surface: Someone is exaggerating how often the post or parcels arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six deliveries, and the over rate is how many overs a side bowls per hour; 'deliveries' suggests the postman, not a bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: To overrate is to rate too highly, so making too much of something is exactly that verb.

clue.text: Play down what’s frequently pinched by lapsed criminal

indicators.note: something pinched is gripped tightly on both sides, so it sits inside the other letters
criminal means crooked or bent, so these letters are twisted out of their order

blocks.note: oft is an old word for often, what happens frequently
taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A former offender minimises the things they used to steal regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinched' suggests theft beside 'criminal', but it only places one piece inside the other; 'lapsed' is not a description but the letters themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: To soft-pedal something is to treat it as less important than it is, from easing off on a piano's soft pedal; that is to play it down.

clue.text: Comfortable, as Carol should be after change of heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, and changing it means its central letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a carol is a song, so it ought to be sung

explanation.surface: Someone called Carol ought to feel at ease once she has had a change of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol looks like a woman's name, but it is a Christmas song; swapping the two middle letters of what a carol should be gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug describes being warm, cosy and at ease, a close synonym for comfortable when talking about a person or a place.

clue.text: Chemical from laminate child regularly picked off

indicators.note: picking at regular intervals means taking every other letter and leaving the rest

blocks.note: Formica is a brand of plastic laminate used on worktops
the first, third and fifth letters of child

explanation.surface: A toxic substance from a kitchen surface was picked off by a child at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: Formica is a trade name for a hard-wearing laminate, common on kitchen worktops in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Formic acid is a simple organic compound found in ant stings, and so it is an example of a chemical.

clue.text: Standard family fare at teatime?

blocks.note: par is the standard or normal level
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: The usual food a household eats at teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: Parkin is a sticky ginger cake made with oatmeal and treacle, traditional in Yorkshire and northern England; the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Parkin is a cake typically eaten with a cup of tea in the afternoon, so it is one example of teatime food.

clue.text: After course, my side’s bearing no shame

indicators.note: coming after means following on, so the pieces are placed one behind the other
to bear is to carry, so one piece carries another inside it

blocks.note: a course of a meal is a dish
what belongs to my side is ours
taken as written

explanation.surface: After a round of the competition, a team member claims their side feels no embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing no shame' reads as one phrase, but 'no' is carried inside OUR, and only 'shame' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishonour is loss of respect or reputation, a disgrace, which is what shame means as a noun.

clue.text: Restraint for dog while a shopper’s absorbed

indicators.note: something absorbed is taken in and lies inside the words around it

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word, the whole of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Tying up a dog outside while its owner is busy shopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absorbed' makes the shopper sound engrossed, but it means the letters are taken in by the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A leash is a lead, a strap or cord attached to a collar to hold an animal back.

clue.text: Old monitor’s spoken of finance office (9)

indicators.note: what is spoken is heard, not seen, so the word is spelt differently from how it sounds

blocks.note: ex means former
someone who monitors checks things

explanation.surface: A former supervisor talks about the finance department where they worked.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exchequer is the British government department responsible for public money, headed by the Chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Exchequer is the government department that collects and manages the national revenue, a finance office on the grandest scale.

clue.text: Believer in return of a former ruler

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the letters run from the end to the start

blocks.note: taken as written
a tsar was an emperor of Russia

explanation.surface: Someone who has faith that an old monarch will come back.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits nicely: Rastafarians revere Haile Selassie, a former emperor of Ethiopia, which is why the clue feels whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Rasta is short for Rastafarian, a follower of a religion founded in Jamaica, and so is a believer.

clue.text: Updated method backed by fighting force

indicators.note: being backed by something means having it right behind, so the pieces follow in order

blocks.note: a mode is a way or manner of doing something
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A new way of doing things is supported by the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: RN, the Royal Navy, is a standard crossword fighting force alongside TA and RA.
explanation.definitionFit: Modern means current or up to date, as something updated has been brought to the present style.

clue.text: Germanic aggressor once shot during stay at hospital

indicators.note: what happens during something falls within it, so one piece sits inside another
being at something means next to it, so the pieces are placed side by side

blocks.note: a visit is a short stay
to have a shot is to have a go
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A German attacker was shot while staying in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' reads as a gunshot wound, but it means an attempt; 'once' belongs to the definition, marking the aggressor as historical.
explanation.definitionFit: The Visigoths were a western Gothic people who invaded the Roman Empire and sacked Rome in 410, a Germanic tribe of old.

clue.text: Party received standard warning of potential takeover bid?

definitions.text: standard warning of potential takeover bid?

blocks.note: a jolly is an informal word for a party or outing
radio operators say roger to mean message received

explanation.surface: A political party receives the usual notice that someone may try to buy the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takeover bid' belongs to boardrooms, but here it is a pirate boarding a ship; a standard is a flag.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jolly Roger is the pirates' skull-and-crossbones flag, flown to warn a ship that it was about to be seized.

clue.text: She’s on set, maybe to KO a couple of staff

blocks.note: a knockout blow stuns
a couple is two
to staff a post is to man it

explanation.surface: An actress on a film set might be about to knock out a couple of crew members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like a noun for employees, but it is the verb meaning to provide workers.
explanation.definitionFit: A stuntwoman performs dangerous action scenes in films, so she works on a set; 'maybe' allows that she is one example.

clue.text: Limited stress good for junior

indicators.note: something limited is kept short of its full extent, so its final letter is cut off

blocks.note: to underline a point is to stress it
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Keeping pressure low is good for a young employee.
explanation.walkthrough: Underline loses its last letter and G for good is added; 'stress' is the verb meaning to emphasise, not strain.
explanation.definitionFit: An underling is a subordinate person of lower rank, which is what a junior is in an organisation.

clue.text: Implement not small enough?

blocks.note: read with 'not small': lacking smallness enough means being too big, so this supplies the excess word
not small is large, and L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Carry out a plan that falls short of being small enough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Implement' looks like a verb meaning to put into effect, but it is the noun for a tool; the rest is read as TOO L, too large.
explanation.definitionFit: An implement is a tool or instrument used for a particular job, such as gardening or cooking.

clue.text: In the course of last year, foolish daughter’s seduced

indicators.note: foolish means silly, and silly letters do not stay in a sensible order
happening in the course of something means inside its span, so one piece lies within another

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent laments that over the past twelve months a silly daughter has been seduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last year' looks like a time phrase, but it is the fodder; D for daughter goes inside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead someone astray is to tempt them into wrongdoing, and seduced here means tempted away from what is right.

clue.text: Vociferous march by conservationists

blocks.note: to stride is to march with long steps
NT is the National Trust, the British heritage and conservation charity

explanation.surface: A noisy protest walk staged by environmental campaigners.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust looks after historic houses and countryside in Britain, which is why conservationists become NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Strident means loud, harsh and insistent, especially of opinions, so it matches vociferous in describing forceful protest.

clue.text: What distinguishes regulated from deregulated crossing

blocks.note: regulated is the shorter word: it has none of the extra prefix
the two letters deregulated carries in front of the shorter word

explanation.surface: Asking what sets a controlled junction apart from an uncontrolled one, like traffic lights.
explanation.walkthrough: The question is not about traffic control at all: take the two words literally and the only difference is a missing DE.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a point where lines or branches meet and intersect, as in a network, so it is a crossing point.

clue.text: Reclusive elector’s ID defective

indicators.note: something defective is faulty or broken, and broken letters are put back in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A voter who keeps to themselves has a faulty identity document.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe's S is part of the fodder, which is easy to overlook.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloistered describes a sheltered life shut away from the world, like a monk in a cloister, which is what reclusive means.

clue.text: Stolen goods ultimately disposed of

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of goods
wiped out means got rid of, disposed of

explanation.surface: Stolen property was eventually got rid of by the thieves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stolen goods' reads as one phrase, loot, but 'Stolen' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Swiped is informal slang for stolen, taken quickly and without permission, as in swiping a purse.

clue.text: Gave up supporting English after recurrent arguments

indicators.note: recurrent literally means running back, so the letters run backwards
coming after means following, so one piece is placed behind the other

blocks.note: to be for something is to support it
rows are quarrels
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone stopped backing the English side after endless disputes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recurrent' suggests arguments that keep happening, but it is read by its roots as running back.
explanation.definitionFit: To forswear something is to renounce it solemnly, promising to abandon it, so the past tense means gave up.

clue.text: Defendant’s third book essential in court case

indicators.note: third names one position in the word, so only the letter standing there is kept

blocks.note: the third letter of defendant
Acts, the Acts of the Apostles, is a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: The accused's third volume of evidence is crucial to the trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defendant's third book' reads as one thing, but 'third' picks a letter and the book is from the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Facts are the established truths a trial is decided on, so they are the essential material of any legal case.

clue.text: Setback for both Irish and East European competitors

indicators.note: set back means moved backwards, and for both means each piece is turned round separately

blocks.note: IR is the abbreviation for Irish
Slavs are a people of eastern Europe

explanation.surface: A defeat hits both the Irish and the East European teams in a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setback' looks like a noun meaning a defeat, but it is read as set back, turning each piece round in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Rivals are people competing for the same prize or goal, so the word is a plain synonym for competitors.

clue.text: Radiant silver-blue

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
feeling blue is feeling low

explanation.surface: A shining silvery-blue colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver-blue' looks like a shade, but the hyphen hides two parts, and blue is the mood, not the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Aglow means glowing with light or warmth, and radiant likewise describes something shining brightly.

clue.text: Grey area reserved

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
a reserved person is shy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grey area' reads as one phrase for something uncertain, but 'Grey' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashy means of the pale whitish colour of ash from a fire, one shade of grey.

clue.text: Treatment from stylist, extremely clever devil

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of clever
an imp is a little devil

explanation.surface: A hairdresser's service praised as the work of a very clever rascal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as an intensifier for clever, but it means the ends of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A crimp is a wave or tight curl put into hair with heated tongs, a styling treatment a hairdresser gives.

clue.text: Preacher‘s an active type, full of charm

indicators.note: something full of a thing holds it inside, so one piece fills the other

blocks.note: a goer is a lively, energetic person
a charm is a magic spell

explanation.surface: A clergyman is described as energetic and full of charisma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charm' sounds like personal appeal, but it is the magical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gospeller is someone who preaches the gospel, an evangelist, so the word names a kind of preacher.

clue.text: Dairy product made by prudent race

blocks.note: a sage person is wise and prudent
the Derby is a famous horse race at Epsom

explanation.surface: A cheese or yoghurt produced by a careful people or nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' suggests a people, but it is a horse race; Sage Derby is an English cheese marbled green with sage.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage Derby is a hard cow's-milk cheese flavoured with sage leaves, and cheese is a dairy product.

clue.text: Colour of any two short bananas

indicators.note: something short falls shy of its full length, so its final letter is lost
going bananas means going crazy, so the letters are scrambled wildly

blocks.note: taken as written
the word two without its last letter

explanation.surface: Asking what colour a pair of undersized bananas might be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the fruit whose colour is sought, but it is slang for crazy and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawny is an orange-brown or yellowish-brown shade, like a lion's coat, so it is one colour.
